subject: surgery
title: Fontaine Classification and Critical Limb Ischaemia

steps.tx: The staging system grading peripheral arterial disease from no symptoms to gangrene is the **Fontaine classification**. Stage one has no symptoms, stage two causes claudication, stage three rest pain and stage four tissue loss. It guides urgency and choice of treatment. Documenting this finding clearly in the notes guides the next clinician and supports safe, well planned further management.
steps.say: The Fontaine classification stages arterial disease from silent narrowing to gangrene and guides treatment urgency.

vis.alt: Fontaine and Rutherford staging of peripheral arterial disease.
vis.caption: Fontaine staging of leg arterial disease. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: Stage two disease limited to walking pain is Fontaine stage **claudication**. Patients remain safe with medical therapy and exercise in most cases. Intervention is reserved for lifestyle limiting symptoms despite best treatment. When this picture is seen in practice, urgent senior review is wise whenever there is any doubt about severity.
steps.say: Fontaine stage two claudication is managed medically with exercise unless lifestyle remains severely limited.

steps.tx: Rest pain with ulcers or gangrene together define **critical limb ischaemia**. Without restoring blood flow, major amputation commonly follows within a year. It is now also called chronic limb threatening ischaemia in modern terminology. Understanding this mechanism explains the symptoms, the investigation findings and the logic behind each step of treatment given.
steps.say: Critical limb ischaemia combines rest pain with tissue loss and commonly leads to amputation without flow restoration.

vis.alt: Advanced peripheral arterial disease with critical ischaemia.
vis.caption: Critical limb ischaemia in arterial disease. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: Widening a narrowed artery from inside with a balloon is **angioplasty**. A stent may hold the vessel open afterwards. It suits short narrowings and avoids a major operation in frail patients. This distinction changes management, so it should be settled early rather than after empirical treatment has already begun.
steps.say: Angioplasty widens narrowed arteries with a balloon and suits short lesions in frail patients.

steps.tx: Bypassing a long blockage with vein or graft is a **surgical bypass**. The patients own vein gives the most durable result for long occlusions. It remains the best option for extensive disease with good targets. Careful history taking and examination help place this finding in the right clinical context before treatment is planned.
steps.say: Surgical bypass with vein gives the most durable result for long arterial blockages.

steps.tx: Choosing between balloon, bypass and amputation needs a **multidisciplinary decision**. Wound extent, infection and patient fitness all weigh in. Preserving a functional foot is the goal whenever realistically possible. Correlating this finding with imaging and laboratory results prevents both delayed treatment and unnecessary intervention in most patients.
steps.say: Multidisciplinary teams weigh wound, infection and fitness to preserve a functional foot whenever possible.

steps.tx: Infection in an ischaemic foot changes everything and demands combined **infection control**. Antibiotics, drainage and urgent flow restoration run together. Operating on blood flow alone while pus spreads invites failure. Early recognition matters because timely treatment gives clearly better outcomes than waiting for complications to develop first.
steps.say: Infected ischaemic feet need antibiotics, drainage and flow restoration together, not flow alone.

steps.tx: Measuring toe pressures helps when ankle vessels are calcified and incompressible, called **toe pressure assessment**. Toes have less calcium, so their pressures reflect true foot perfusion better in diabetics. It refines amputation level decisions too. Students should connect this fact with the presenting symptoms, since examination questions usually test that clinical link directly.
steps.say: Toe pressures reflect true foot perfusion better when ankle vessels are calcified in diabetics.

steps.tx: After any revascularisation, long term success depends on continued **secondary prevention**. Antiplatelet drugs, statins, diabetes control and smoking cessation protect the whole circulation. Graft surveillance catches narrowings before they thrombose. Documenting this finding clearly in the notes guides the next clinician and supports safe, well planned further management.
steps.say: Secondary prevention with antiplatelets, statins and surveillance protects grafts and the whole circulation.
